questions.question: What is the difference between std::sort and std::stable_sort?
options: sort does NOT preserve equal-element order — O(n log n); stable_sort DOES preserve equal-element order — O(n log² n); use stable_sort when relative order of equals matters
sort is stable; stable_sort is unstable
questions.answer: sort does NOT preserve equal-element order — O(n log n); stable_sort DOES preserve equal-element order — O(n log² n); use stable_sort when relative order of equals matters

questions.question: What is the difference between std::map and std::unordered_map?
options: std::map is a sorted red-black tree with O(log n) operations; std::unordered_map uses hashing with O(1) average — use map for sorted iteration, unordered_map for speed
unordered_map is slower than map for all operations
map allows duplicate keys; unordered_map does not
questions.answer: std::map is a sorted red-black tree with O(log n) operations; std::unordered_map uses hashing with O(1) average — use map for sorted iteration, unordered_map for speed

questions.question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle and how does it relate to C++ inheritance?
options: LSP states that base classes must always be abstract

LSP: objects of a derived class must be substitutable for base class objects without altering correctness — derived classes must honour the base contract (no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions)
LSP only applies to multiple inheritance
LSP is enforced by the C++ compiler
questions.answer: LSP: objects of a derived class must be substitutable for base class objects without altering correctness — derived classes must honour the base contract (no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions)

questions.question: What is the One Definition Rule (ODR) in C++ and what happens when it is violated?
options: ODR requires every variable to be defined in exactly one header
ODR: every non-inline function, variable, or class must have exactly one definition across all translation units — violations cause linker errors (multiple definition) or undefined behavior
ODR only applies to class member functions
ODR is automatically enforced with no programmer responsibility
questions.answer: ODR: every non-inline function, variable, or class must have exactly one definition across all translation units — violations cause linker errors (multiple definition) or undefined behavior

push_back adds multiple elements; emplace_back only one

questions.question: What is the difference between std::string and a C-style char array?
options: They are identical — std::string is typedef for char*
std::string is a class with automatic memory management, size tracking, and rich API; C-style strings are null-terminated char arrays requiring manual memory management — prone to buffer overflows
std::string cannot be passed to C library functions
questions.answer: std::string is a class with automatic memory management, size tracking, and rich API; C-style strings are null-terminated char arrays requiring manual memory management — prone to buffer overflows

questions.question: What is a functor in C++ and how is it used with STL algorithms?
options: A functor is a function pointer stored in a variable
A functor is an object of a class overloading operator() — passed to STL algorithms like sort/transform; can maintain state between calls unlike plain function pointers
questions.answer: A functor is an object of a class overloading operator() — passed to STL algorithms like sort/transform; can maintain state between calls unlike plain function pointers

questions.question: What are the differences between std::array and a raw C-style array?
options: std::array is slower for all operations
std::array knows its size (size()), supports iterators, range-for, and STL algorithms, and does not decay to pointer; raw arrays decay to pointers losing size information
Raw arrays support more STL algorithms

questions.question: What is the purpose of explicit on a conversion operator?

questions.question: What is the difference between a using declaration and a using directive in C++?
options: Identical — both import all namespace names
using declaration (using std::cout) imports one specific name; using directive (using namespace std) imports all names — directive risks name conflicts, declaration is safer

questions.question: What is a variadic template in C++11?
options: Accepts zero or more template parameters using ... syntax — enables generic functions for any number/type of arguments; used in std::tuple, std::make_unique, perfect forwarding

questions.question: What is perfect forwarding in C++11?
options: std::forward<T> with universal references (T&&) passes arguments preserving their value category (lvalue stays lvalue, rvalue stays rvalue) — avoids unnecessary copies in generic wrappers like make_unique
questions.answer: std::forward<T> with universal references (T&&) passes arguments preserving their value category (lvalue stays lvalue, rvalue stays rvalue) — avoids unnecessary copies in generic wrappers like make_unique

questions.question: What is a smart pointer and why prefer it over raw pointers?
options: Smart pointers are slower and should be avoided
Smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr) automatically manage heap object lifetimes — call delete when appropriate, preventing leaks and dangling pointers; work correctly with exceptions
Smart pointers only usable with STL containers

questions.question: What is the difference between constexpr and const in C++11?
options: constexpr guarantees compile-time evaluation — usable in array sizes, template arguments, case labels; const only promises no runtime modification but may be runtime-initialized
const is compile-time; constexpr is runtime
questions.answer: constexpr guarantees compile-time evaluation — usable in array sizes, template arguments, case labels; const only promises no runtime modification but may be runtime-initialized
